groups.title: Topics and partitions
groups.mechanism: A topic is divided into ordered partitions. Ordering is local to a partition, and keys influence placement under producer partitioning behavior.
groups.tradeOff: More partitions increase parallelism while affecting ordering, overhead and migration assumptions.
groups.verify: Produce related and unrelated keys, inspect placement and test consumer ordering.

questions.question: What is a Kafka topic?
questions.answer: A named stream divided into partitions with configured storage, replication and retention behavior.

questions.question: What is a partition offset?
questions.answer: A position within one partition's log; it is not a global topic sequence or universal business operation identity.

questions.question: When should messages share a key?
questions.answer: When they need consistent partition affinity under the chosen partitioning contract, often to preserve per-entity processing order.

questions.question: Why can increasing partition count alter key routing?
questions.answer: The partitioner's mapping can change as the available partition set changes, affecting affinity assumptions for later records.

questions.question: How would you choose a partition count?
questions.answer: Balance throughput, key distribution, consumer concurrency, broker overhead and future growth, then test realistic hot-key traffic.

groups.title: Brokers and replication
groups.mechanism: Partition leaders serve requests while replicas maintain copies according to Kafka's replication model. ISR and producer acknowledgment settings jointly affect accepted-write behavior.
groups.tradeOff: Availability, durability and latency depend on several aligned settings rather than replication factor alone.
groups.verify: Fail leaders and replicas under the intended acknowledgment and ISR configuration.

questions.question: What is the role of a Kafka broker?
questions.answer: Hosting partitions and participating in storage, replication and client request handling within the cluster.

questions.question: How does replication factor differ from minimum in-sync replicas?
questions.answer: Replication factor defines copies; min.insync.replicas constrains required ISR size for applicable writes, notably with the relevant producer acknowledgment configuration.

questions.question: What does acks=all mean?
questions.answer: The producer waits for acknowledgment according to the current in-sync replica set and broker rules, not every configured replica regardless of state.

questions.question: Why can unsafe leader election threaten acknowledged data?
questions.answer: Selecting a replica lacking the latest accepted records can make previously acknowledged data unavailable or lost under the failure scenario.

questions.question: How would you evaluate durability settings?
questions.answer: Combine replication, ISR policy, acknowledgments, election behavior and operational failures, then measure accepted-write survival and availability trade-offs.

groups.title: Producer behavior
groups.mechanism: Producers serialize records, select partitions, batch sends and observe acknowledgments. Delivery timeouts and retries can leave application-level uncertainty.
groups.tradeOff: Batching improves throughput while increasing latency or outstanding memory.
groups.verify: Test serialization failure, unavailable brokers, lost acknowledgments and bounded flush/close behavior.

questions.question: Why does a Kafka producer batch records?
questions.answer: To amortize network and processing overhead across records going to appropriate destinations, subject to latency and memory settings.

questions.question: When is compression useful?
questions.answer: When reduced network and storage work outweigh compression CPU and latency costs for the actual payload distribution.

questions.question: How do delivery timeout and request timeout differ?
questions.answer: They cover different producer timing boundaries; configure the full operation budget rather than treating one setting as every possible wait.

questions.question: Why can a send callback report failure after the application lost certainty?
questions.answer: The record may have reached the broker before acknowledgment or timeout handling completed; reconcile according to producer and operation identity semantics.

questions.question: How would you operate a high-throughput producer?
questions.answer: Reuse the supported producer safely, bound buffered work, observe errors and latency, and test ordering plus duplicate behavior under retries.

groups.title: Idempotent producers and transactions
groups.mechanism: Kafka producer idempotence and transactions protect defined Kafka-side scopes. They do not automatically deduplicate a user's repeated business requests or atomically include an external database.
groups.tradeOff: Stronger Kafka coordination adds configuration and lifecycle requirements.
groups.verify: Crash between database commit, Kafka send and transaction completion.

questions.question: What does producer idempotence protect against?
questions.answer: Duplicates caused by supported producer retry behavior within Kafka's producer protocol scope, subject to required configuration and lifecycle semantics.

questions.question: When are Kafka transactions useful?
questions.answer: For atomic Kafka record publication and supported offset coordination in Kafka-centric processing workflows.

questions.question: What does read_committed change for a consumer?
questions.answer: It restricts visibility according to Kafka transaction commitment semantics, rather than exposing records from aborted transactions as ordinary committed data.

questions.question: Why does exactly-once Kafka processing not guarantee exactly-once payment?
questions.answer: The payment provider is outside Kafka's transaction boundary, and application retries can represent new external attempts.

questions.question: How would you integrate Kafka with a relational write?
questions.answer: Use an outbox/inbox or another explicit coordination protocol, durable business keys and recovery tests for each cross-system uncertainty window.

groups.title: Consumer groups and ownership
groups.mechanism: A group assigns partitions among participating consumers under its protocol. Ownership can change, and external effects must remain safe when a former owner is delayed.
groups.tradeOff: Parallel consumers improve throughput only up to partition and workload limits.
groups.verify: Trigger reassignment during active work and verify no skipped or duplicated business effects.

questions.question: What does a consumer group provide?
questions.answer: Coordinated partition consumption for a logical subscriber, distributing partition ownership among group members under supported protocol rules.

questions.question: Can adding more consumers than partitions increase active partition parallelism?
questions.answer: Not for ordinary group assignment; some consumers can remain without partitions while other bottlenecks still limit throughput.

questions.question: What happens during a rebalance?
questions.answer: Partition ownership changes, requiring the application to handle outstanding work and progress according to its supported consumer integration.

questions.question: Why should a KafkaConsumer not be casually shared across threads?
questions.answer: Its threading contract is restricted; use an intentional poll/processing architecture and supported coordination rather than concurrent arbitrary access.

questions.question: How would you prevent stale consumers from applying unsafe effects?
questions.answer: Use durable idempotency or storage-enforced ownership/version rules, and coordinate revocation with pending work without assuming interruption stops it.

groups.title: Offsets and acknowledgments
groups.mechanism: Committed offsets describe a consumer's restart position. Application processing completion and durable business effects are separate events.
groups.tradeOff: Early commits improve apparent progress while risking loss; late commits create duplicate windows.
groups.verify: Crash before and after the effect and before and after the offset commit.

questions.question: What does committing a consumer offset mean?
questions.answer: Recording the position from which the group should resume under Kafka's offset convention; it is not proof of an external business commit.

questions.question: Why is commit-before-process risky?
questions.answer: A crash after committing progress but before completing the effect can prevent the unfinished record from being redelivered normally.

questions.question: Why is process-before-commit still duplicate-prone?
questions.answer: The effect can commit while offset acknowledgment fails, so the record is processed again after restart.

questions.question: How can out-of-order completion skip work?
questions.answer: Committing beyond an unfinished earlier record advances the restart position past that record in the same partition.

questions.question: How would you track safe progress with parallel workers?
questions.answer: Preserve partition ordering or maintain a supported contiguous completed prefix with bounded in-flight work and explicit revocation behavior.

groups.title: Retention and compaction
groups.mechanism: Retention removes data by configured policies; compaction retains key-oriented history according to its asynchronous rules. Neither means every historical record remains forever.
groups.tradeOff: Storage controls can conflict with replay and lagging-consumer recovery needs.
groups.verify: Run lagging readers and rebuild projections while applying the actual retention policy.

questions.question: How does time/size retention differ from compaction?
questions.answer: Retention removes eligible log segments; compaction reduces older keyed records according to key-history rules while preserving supported latest-state semantics.

questions.question: What is a tombstone in a compacted topic?
questions.answer: A keyed record with a null value used to represent deletion under compaction and retention rules.

questions.question: Does compaction immediately leave exactly one record per key?
questions.answer: No. It is asynchronous and readers can encounter multiple versions before cleaning occurs.

questions.question: Why can a slow consumer lose its replay opportunity?
questions.answer: Required records can age out or be removed before the consumer processes or rebuilds from them.

questions.question: How would you select retention for recovery?
questions.answer: Cover expected outages, replay duration and audit needs, budget storage and monitor lag against the remaining recovery horizon.

groups.title: Schemas and event evolution
groups.mechanism: Serialization defines the durable contract understood by producers and consumers. Schema compatibility checks do not prove preserved business meaning.
groups.tradeOff: Flexible evolution reduces synchronized deployment but requires historical replay testing.
groups.verify: Read old events with new code and supported new events with old consumers.

questions.question: Why use an explicit event schema?
questions.answer: To define field types and compatibility expectations independently of incidental implementation objects.

questions.question: When is adding an optional field safe?
questions.answer: When supported readers tolerate it and its default or absence preserves meaning; verify both schema rules and application behavior.

questions.question: Why should event timestamps specify meaning?
questions.answer: Creation, business occurrence and ingestion time can differ, affecting windows, ordering and reconciliation.

questions.question: What breaks when an event key changes casually?
questions.answer: Partition affinity, compaction identity and downstream deduplication can all change even if the value schema is unchanged.

questions.question: How would you version an incompatible event?
questions.answer: Introduce an explicit new contract with consumer migration, replay handling and a retirement plan for retained old data.

groups.title: Poison messages and retries
groups.mechanism: Repeated failures can block partition progress or create uncontrolled retry traffic. Quarantine requires durable evidence and a safe relationship to acknowledgment.
groups.tradeOff: Skipping preserves availability but can violate ordering or leave business state incomplete.
groups.verify: Inject malformed and permanently invalid records, then fail the quarantine destination itself.

questions.question: What is a poison message?
questions.answer: A record that repeatedly fails processing under the current contract, often because the failure is permanent rather than transient.

questions.question: When should a message be quarantined?
questions.answer: After a deliberate classification and retry policy, retaining enough identity and diagnostic context for safe correction or replay.

questions.question: Why can a dead-letter path still lose a record?
questions.answer: If progress is acknowledged before quarantine is durably accepted, failure can leave neither normal processing nor recoverable quarantine evidence.

questions.question: How do retry topics affect ordering?
questions.answer: Moving one record aside can let later records proceed, so per-key business ordering may no longer match the original partition sequence.

questions.question: How would you design a safe replay tool?
questions.answer: Authorize scope, preserve business idempotency, validate corrected payloads and track replay identity plus outcomes without blindly repeating irreversible effects.

groups.title: Security and operations
groups.mechanism: Kafka authorization, transport identity and encryption protect different boundaries. Operational health includes lag age, processing success and broker resource pressure.
groups.tradeOff: More telemetry helps diagnosis but payload logging can expose sensitive business data.
groups.verify: Test denied topic actions, credential rotation, broker failure and consumer backlog recovery.

questions.question: What should Kafka ACLs restrict?
questions.answer: The actions and resources a principal may use, including relevant topic, group and transactional capabilities under the deployment's security model.

questions.question: Why is consumer lag alone insufficient?
questions.answer: An offset difference does not directly express record age, processing cost or whether external effects are correct.

questions.question: When does adding consumers fail to reduce lag?
questions.answer: Partitions, hot keys, slow dependencies or processing failures can remain the bottleneck regardless of extra group members.

questions.question: Why can large fetches exhaust application memory?
questions.answer: Fetched records, deserialized objects and queued worker tasks can accumulate beyond the intended in-flight bound.

questions.question: How would you diagnose a growing backlog?
questions.answer: Compare ingress rate, processing throughput, record age, partition skew, errors and dependency latency, then verify a bounded recovery rate without overloading downstream systems.
